extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers of Russian/Soviet humour; translators and comedians seeking characteristics of Russian jokes
extracted.subtask_description: Describing the features, archetypes, formats, and cultural/linguistic devices that define Russian (Soviet) jokes (anekdoty), to guide analysis or composition of authentic examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punch line
rubrics_metrics.description: Russian jokes are short fictional stories or dialogs with a punch line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article opens by defining anekdoty as short stories/dialogs whose humour depends on a punch line; many examples throughout end with a single striking line that resolves the set-up. Emphasize a concise, often surprising final sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shortness and format (two-liners, dialogues, short narratives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many Russian jokes are very short — two-liners, quick dialogues, or brief narratives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several archetypes (eg. Stierlitz, many student/teacher jokes) are typically two-line spoofs; others use brief dialog formats (question–answer, exam bilet format). Economy of text and swift set-up/punchline timing are central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed settings and recurring characters (archetypes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Russian joke culture includes categories with fixed settings and characters (archetypes) that carry expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece stresses that each category (eg. named characters, animals, ethnic types, professions) has an established background allowing instant recognition and predictable interplay; using an archetype signals expected behavior and punchline templates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence on linguistic features, puns and wordplay (marked with (L))
rubrics_metrics.description: Many jokes rely on linguistic puns, wordplay, and Russian-language-specific vocabulary; such jokes may be untranslatable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that (L) marks jokes whose humour critically depends on Russian-language features. Translators should expect loss of effect; writers can exploit homophones, affixation, and grammar to create humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of taboo vocabulary (mat) and its morphological productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Obscene Russian vocabulary (mat) often enhances the humour; Russian morphology allows many derivations from a few mat roots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taboo words can provide emotional impact or function as versatile lexical building blocks. Examples include polite-turned-vulgar inversions and exploitation of mat affixation; cultural sensitivity and untranslatability are noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethnic and regional stereotyping as a device
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethnic stereotypes (Chukchi, Ukrainians, Georgians, Jews, Chinese, Finns/Estonians, etc.) are a common basis for jokes, using perceived traits and accents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article catalogues many ethnic categories and their characteristic traits (e.g., Chukchi: simple-minded but clever; Ukrainians: rustic, fond of salo; Georgians: theatrical, greedy). Accents, invented names, and cultural clichés are used to signal and deliver punchlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political subtext and satire
rubrics_metrics.description: A major subcategory is political jokes that comment on Soviet/Russian authorities, bureaucracy, and policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political jokes can be direct satire, indirect allegory (animals, fables), or topical references (Chernobyl, Five Year Plans). They often rely on double meaning and can serve as social critique or coping mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character voice, mimicry and film/TV reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes often mimic distinctive voices or lines from film/TV and rely on audience recognition of performance traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Stierlitz jokes spoof the solemn TV voice-over; Sherlock Holmes jokes imitate Livanov's husky voice and canonical lines ('Elementary, Watson'). Performance and delivery (voice imitation, timing) are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue templates (teacher–pupil, doctor–patient, exam bilet)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several recurring joke forms are dialogic templates: teacher–student (Vovochka), doctor–patient, exam-ticket (bilet) exchanges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These templates set up roles and moral/authority relationships that the punchline subverts (eg. pupil gives obscene answer, student cheats/khalyava). The exam bilet format generates many stock set-ups and punchlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal fable structure with a moral maxim
rubrics_metrics.description: Animal jokes function like fables: anthropomorphized animals with stereotypical behaviours leading to a punchline that often reads as a maxim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Animals carry predictable gender/roles (Wolf male, Fox female, Bear simple-minded). Punchlines often crystallize a folk maxim or satirical observation (eg. 'try to prove you are not a camel').

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-wishes / Golden Fish / Genie template
rubrics_metrics.description: A common plot uses a wish-granting being (Golden Fish/Genie) where the third wish produces the punchline, often exposing greed or stupidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article traces this to Pushkin and notes variations: the fisherman vs representative of a nationality; cultural expectations (eg. 'three' as convivial number) shape the joke's twist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intertextuality and parody of literary/historical characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes frequently reuse well-known literary, historical, or cinematic characters (Rzhevsky, Chapayev, Sherlock Holmes, bogatyrs) to generate contrast and humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of high-culture figures in low-comic situations (eg. Rzhevsky with Natasha Rostova) creates incongruity. Knowledge of the source material heightens audience appreciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catchphrases and stock lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain lines become catchphrases and are reused across jokes to signify an archetype or punchline motif.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Gusary deneg ne berut!', 'Гусары, молчать!'. These signals let tellers compress context and play on shared cultural memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Politeness inversion and incongruity (substituting politeness for expected profanity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A recurrent device is replacing an expected profane or emotional response with an excessively polite or bureaucratic one for comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include the injured worker who issues a polite safety rebuke instead of swearing. This inversion creates surprise and social critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topicality and historical reference (Chernobyl, Five Year Plans, 1990s New Russians)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many jokes respond to or incorporate contemporary events, social phenomena, or historical episodes to create immediacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article includes sections on Chernobyl jokes, 'vicious 90s' (New Russians), and Soviet-era Five Year Plan parodies; topical knowledge increases impact but dates the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-deprecating and national self-stereotyping
rubrics_metrics.description: Russians often appear as the butt of their own jokes — self-irony depicting simplicity, resourcefulness, or brute force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Russians outwit technologically superior foreigners with cleverness or force. This allows communal bonding and diffuses shame through humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurdism, literal-minded misinterpretation and anti-climax
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour frequently arises from absurd literal conclusions, non sequiturs or anti-climactic deductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Stierlitz deducing a refrigerator; Holmes' camping tent being stolen as the 'deduction'. Writers use literal-mindedness or grotesque misreading to land the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-jokes, repetition and call–response
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jokes use iterative repetition or group-response as a built-in gag (meta-jokes that riff on their own pattern).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Rzhevsky 'arse' sequence and Hussar chorus are meta-jokes where audience expectation of repetition is the humour source; timing and escalation matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammatical/gendered language features as comedic tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Russian grammatical gender and other language-specific features are exploited for characterization and wordplay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes expectations about animal genders and how features like long vowels or lack of genders (Estonian) contribute to accented imitation or stereotype-based jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bureaucratic and procedural parody
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes parody bureaucracy, paperwork, and institutional absurdities (eg. proving you are not a camel; official inspections).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bureaucratic formats and legalistic language are ripe for inversion; many Soviet-era jokes target the presumption of guilt, lishenets, or official forms and procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance and delivery (timing, voice, cultural framing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective jokes depend on oral performance: timing, intonation, voice imitation, and assumed shared cultural framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many examples rely on mimicry (actors' voices, accents), deliberate pauses, and audience knowledge; printed text may annotate (L) or indicate voice for live performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stierlitz archetype: solemn two-liner, parody of TV voice‑over
rubrics_metrics.description: Stierlitz jokes spoof the solemn style of the Seventeen Moments of Spring TV voice-overs; typically two-liners resolved by grotesque wordplay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show deadpan narration and anticlimax (refrigerator deduction). To write in this mode, mimic the original's gravity and subvert it with triviality or absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poruchik Rzhevsky archetype: vulgar hussar, sexual bluntness with high-society contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: Rzhevsky is a hussar officer: straightforward, unsophisticated, rudely sexual but often avoiding heavy mat; his vulgarity contrasts with high society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jokes exploit sexual bluntness, catchphrases, and a running gag of 'arse' answers; maintain his casual bravado and the clash with genteel settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rabinovich archetype: Jewish wit and self-deprecation
rubrics_metrics.description: Rabinovich is the Jewish protagonist of many Soviet jokes characterized by cynicism, self-irony and clever retorts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include ironic remarks about bureaucracy, emigration, or political elites; the voice often imitates a Jewish accent and Odesa-style humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vovochka archetype (Little Johnny): schoolboy giving adult/obscene wisecracks
rubrics_metrics.description: Vovochka is a 'Little Johnny' figure who interacts with a female teacher (Maria Ivanovna) and gives adult, often obscene, punchlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The device is juxtaposing childlike persona with adult lewdness or literalness; many such jokes became politically sensitive post-2000s.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vasily Ivanovich Chapayev archetype: Red Army commander with Petka and Anka
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapayev jokes revolve around war, military incompetence, and comic misunderstandings, usually featuring Petka and Anka.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They parody Bolshevik heroism and military life; expect banter between commander and sidekicks and punchlines that undercut official narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sherlock Holmes and Dr Watson variant: ‘logical’ deductions misapplied
rubrics_metrics.description: These jokes borrow Holmes/Watson roles, applying hyper-rational deductions to absurdly ordinary situations for a twist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mimicking canonical lines (e.g., 'Elementary, Watson') and producing an anti-climactic deduction (tent stolen) are typical. Audience familiarity with Holmes heightens effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantômas and disguise jokes: humour from mastery of disguise
rubrics_metrics.description: Fantômas-type jokes play on a master-of-disguise motif, enabling cross-character surprises and unexpected identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The punchline often comes from revealing the disguised identity or using disguise to comment on geopolitics or sexual affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bogatyrs / folk-hero parody
rubrics_metrics.description: Bogatyr jokes use folk-hero figures (Ilya Muromets, Dobrynya) reimagined as arrogant or cunning in modern comic scenarios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These juxtapose epic heroism with petty modern conflicts; humour comes from anachronism and role reversal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Armenian Radio (Radio Yerevan) Q&A template
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes beginning 'The Armenian Radio was asked...' where the answer is unexpectedly discouraging or ironic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This Q&A format is a stock template producing irony via an authoritative-sounding but subversive response; brevity and deadpan tone are typical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drunkards and policemen as occupational joke types
rubrics_metrics.description: Occupational stereotypes (drunks, militsioner/police) are common: drunks for slapstick and resourcefulness, police for bribery/stupidity jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect setups emphasizing drunken logic, invented codes (e.g., 'book' = 'vodka'), or corrupt policing (portable stop sign gag). These are staples of Soviet/Russian sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: University student / exam culture jokes (khalyava, zachyotka, stipend)
rubrics_metrics.description: Student jokes lampoon dorm life, food shortages, exam bilet rituals, and the culture of 'khalyava' (getting by without effort).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common motifs: last-minute cramming, partying before exams, odd canteen behaviour. These jokes rely on shared student experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cowboy / imported-genre parody
rubrics_metrics.description: A subset imitates Wild West tropes (cowboys, Texas) filtered through Russian sensibilities and anti-climax humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These may be borrowed or adapted; humour arises from mismatch between genre expectations and Russian practicality or deadpan responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disabilities and mental hospital jokes (political or cruel variants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes set in mental hospitals often carry political subtext (who is sane under a regime) and exploit absurd diagnostic tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some such jokes are politically pointed (lecture about communism in asylum) and may be sensitive; they use role inversion and absurd criteria to satirize institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taboo vocabulary as metajoke and morphological resource
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond shock value, mat itself is sometimes the subject: jokes exploit taboo status or morphological productivity to create layers of humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include polite substitutes for expected profanity, invented compound names that produce obscene phrases, and jokes that comment on the taboo nature of mat.
